passage: I'm Chaitanya, the helper in Pradeep sir's nursery class. Gunjan came back on Monday, a week after her Dada died. She ran straight to the sand tray and built a castle, laughing, as if nothing had happened. Then at colouring time her red crayon snapped. She sobbed and sobbed, face in her arms. Pradeep sir knelt beside her. 'You're very sad. I'm here.' He gave her a new crayon and kept the day's routine the same. By snack time she was playing again.

qa.q: What did Gunjan build when she came back?
qa.a: She built a castle in the sand tray.

qa.q: Why might a snapped crayon make Gunjan sob so hard?
qa.a: Her big sadness about Dada may come out in short bursts, and a small loss like a crayon can let it spill over.

qa.q: What did Pradeep sir do that helps a grieving young child?
qa.a: He named her sadness in simple words, stayed close, gave her a new crayon and kept the routine steady.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt watching Gunjan go from laughing to sobbing?
qa.a: Chaitanya may have been surprised and moved, not knowing what Gunjan felt inside but seeing how fast her mood changed.

grounding: A classroom helper sees a young girl back after a bereavement play normally, then sob over a broken crayon, and the teacher respond with simple words and routine.

passage:
Tuesday: Madhav came back to class after his Nani's funeral and zoomed his toy car around as if nothing had happened. Sumit sir let him.
Thursday: Madhav's crayon broke in half. He threw it and wailed, "It's broken! It's all broken!" Sumit sir sat beside him. "You feel very sad. Nani died, and that is very sad." Madhav leaned on his arm.
The next Monday: Madhav drew a house with a big sun. "That's Nani's house," he said, then ran off to the swings.

qa.q: What did Madhav do with his toy car on Tuesday?
qa.a: He zoomed his toy car around as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: What might Madhav's wail 'It's all broken!' show about his feelings?
qa.a: His grief about Nani may have come out through the broken crayon, a short burst of the big sadness he couldn't put into words.

qa.q: Which of Sumit sir's choices helps most at this stage?
qa.a: Using simple, honest words about Nani's death and sitting beside Madhav, while letting normal play and routine continue.

qa.q: How might Sumit sir feel when Madhav says 'That's Nani's house' and runs off?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and tender, seeing Madhav mention Nani calmly and then go back to play.

grounding: Over several days a teacher sees a young boy play as if nothing happened after a death, then cry over a crayon, and helps with simple words and routine.

passage:
It was the first day back after the holidays the helper was absent, so Usha ma'am had thirty-two children alone, with rain drumming on the roof.
Vishal came in holding his father's hand. His Dadi had died two weeks ago. Usha watched him. He ran to the block corner, built a tall tower, laughed when it fell.
At drawing time, his green crayon snapped. Vishal stared at it, and then he was sobbing, huge sobs, far bigger than a crayon.
Usha knelt beside him and held out her hand. "It broke. That's sad. I'm here." He leaned into her. A minute later he was drawing again, with blue.

qa.q: What colour was the crayon that snapped?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What might Usha ma'am have been feeling as she watched Vishal laugh at the tower?
qa.a: She was probably watchful and a little puzzled, knowing about his Dadi yet seeing him play as if nothing had happened.

qa.q: What helped Vishal most in this moment?
qa.a: Usha kneeling beside him with short, simple words and her calm presence, then letting him go back to drawing.

qa.q: What is it like for Vishal when the crayon breaks?
qa.a: The small loss seems to open up his big sadness about Dadi, which comes out in a short burst of sobbing.

grounding: Shows a teacher watching a young child play normally after a bereavement, then sob over a broken crayon, and responding with simple words.

passage:
In the Chennai nursery class, Charu ma'am kept the morning exactly as usual: songs, snack, story. Ritu had come back that Monday after her Thatha's funeral.
Ritu sang loudly. She shared her biscuits. She played shop with her friends and laughed. Charu wondered if Ritu understood what had happened at all.
Then, at colouring time, Ritu's favourite pink crayon broke in half. Ritu burst into tears and wouldn't stop. "It's broken! It's broken!"
Charu sat on the small chair beside her. "Your crayon broke. You're very sad." She didn't say more. She just stayed.
After a few minutes, Ritu wiped her nose and asked for the orange one.

qa.q: Which crayon broke?
qa.a: Ritu's favourite pink crayon.

qa.q: What was Charu ma'am feeling as Ritu sang and played?
qa.a: She felt uncertain and a little worried, wondering if Ritu understood her Thatha's death.

qa.q: Which of Charu ma'am's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the usual routine and using simple words without a lecture, because that gave Ritu safety for her short burst of grief.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu when the crayon breaks?
qa.a: It seems to let out sadness she couldn't show before, in a short, strong burst before she returns to play.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a young child playing normally after a bereavement, then crying over a broken crayon, and keeping routine and simple words.

passage:
"Uma, welcome back," said Lakshmi ma'am.
"I made a car at home!" Uma ran straight to the sand tray.
At lunch, Uma chattered about the car. She didn't mention her Nani, who had died last week. Lakshmi ma'am watched quietly.
At art time Uma's crayon snapped.
"NO!" Uma burst into tears.
"Oh, Uma. It broke."
"I want it fixed! I want it back!"
"I know. Some things can't be fixed. It's okay to be sad."
"Nani can't come back."
"No, she can't. That's very sad."
Uma cried into Lakshmi ma'am's sari. Then she picked up a new crayon.

qa.q: Where did Uma run when she arrived?
qa.a: Straight to the sand tray.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi ma'am feeling when Uma said "Nani can't come back"?
qa.a: She seemed calm but moved and caring, answering honestly and gently.

qa.q: Why were Lakshmi ma'am's short, honest words helpful?
qa.a: They matched what Uma could take in, naming sadness simply without false promises.

qa.q: What is it like for Uma when the crayon snaps?
qa.a: It opens up her grief about Nani in a short burst, and she needs comfort before going back to play.

grounding: Shows a teacher seeing a young child play normally after a death, then cry over a broken crayon, and answering with simple, honest words.

passage:
Teacher's note, UKG-B, Monday.
Dhruv came back today after ten days away; his Nani died last month. He ran straight to the sand tray, built a road and laughed with the others as if nothing had changed. At snack time his green crayon snapped. He cried hard, shoulders shaking. I sat beside him and said, "Crayons break. It's okay to feel sad. I'm here." He leaned on me for a few minutes, then picked up the half crayon. I kept our usual routine all day and will tell his mother at pickup what happened.
Kalyani

qa.q: What happened at snack time?
qa.a: Dhruv's green crayon snapped and he cried hard.

qa.q: What does Kalyani seem to feel when Dhruv cries over the crayon?
qa.a: Kalyani seems caring and concerned, staying calm beside him and sensing the tears are about more than a crayon.

qa.q: What helped Dhruv here?
qa.a: Simple words, sitting close and keeping the usual routine gave him a safe, steady place to feel sad.

qa.q: What might the broken crayon be like for Dhruv?
qa.a: A small loss lets out the big sadness about his Nani that did not show while he was playing.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a young child playing normally after a death, then crying over a broken crayon, and responding with routine and simple words.
